name: Vera Evans

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time today. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're independent, with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you tell me is confidential, and your name won't be attached to anything. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Most weeks I do day calls for Meadowbank Homecare around the villages outside the market town, but about once a month I do a live-in respite week. That's when I move into someone's home for seven days so the husband or daughter who normally cares for them can have a break. Right now it's day calls: Mr Achterberg at eight, who's deaf, so I've been learning sign language with an AI app on my phone. I like the live-in weeks best, because you actually get to know someone. What wears me out is the driving between villages, it's forty miles some days.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: You mentioned learning sign language with an AI app. Do you use AI much otherwise?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Every day. I use it to plan my routes, to keep track of my mileage claims, and to explain a client's new diagnosis in normal words before I see the nurse. I share a flat with my friend Priya, who's a hairdresser, and she calls me the robot whisperer. I've only got a couple of weeks' money saved, though, so I'm not exactly winning at life yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bit disappointing. I'd half hoped AI would sort out the driving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's useful, just not magic, which is what I think about most things. I'd tell friends to keep using the bits that save time and stop waiting for a miracle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately it means I'm still on low pay with forty-mile days and a couple of weeks of savings. Meadowbank's fine as a company, they're not going bust, so my job's safe. But the car costs eat everything, and there aren't many other agencies round here to play off against each other.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do more live-in respite weeks, because they pay a flat rate and I'm not spending on fuel that week. I'd keep using AI to tighten my routes and claim every mile I'm owed. And I'd look into registering as a self-employed carer for one or two private families, for extra money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine, a bit frustrated. Like I'm running hard on the same spot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much do the claimed miles actually add up to?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Since I started tracking my mileage properly with the AI, I get about thirty more a month. It sounds small, but it's my phone bill. I used to just forget half of them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is self-employed work a big risk for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. No sick pay, and you have to do your own tax. But I'd only take one family at first, alongside Meadowbank. If it went wrong, I'd still have the agency.

say: I'd say AI is **useful, not magic**.
I'd tell friends to **keep using time-savers** and stop waiting for miracles.
think: I think my **job's safe**, but I'm still on low pay.
**Car costs** eat everything, and there are **few agencies** nearby.
do: Take more **live-in respite weeks**, which save on fuel.
Use AI to **claim every mile**, worth about thirty a month.
Register as **self-employed** for one private family alongside Meadowbank.
feel: **Frustrated**, like running hard on the same spot.
S0.quote: Since I started tracking my mileage properly with the AI, I get about thirty more a month. It sounds small, but it's my phone bill.
fieldNote: She uses AI **practically**, for routes, mileage and understanding diagnoses.
Her worry is **low pay and fuel**, not job loss.
She'd take a **measured risk** on private work while keeping the agency job.

steps.text: Book more live-in respite weeks for the flat rate
Claim every mile owed using her AI mileage tracker
Register as self-employed and take one private family

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That actually sounds like my kind of change. The thinking work goes, and I'm already using it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the carers who learn the tools will be fine, and the ones who don't will struggle. I'd say it nicely, but I'd say it. I'd probably offer to show people at Meadowbank how I do my routes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think it helps me more than it hurts. The office would get smaller, and matching carers to families could go to apps, which makes private work easier for someone like me. The risk is the apps take a big cut, like the taxi ones do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd join one of the care-matching apps for weekend private work, but read the small print on the fees first. I'd offer Meadowbank a short session on route planning with AI for the other carers. And I'd save whatever the private work brings in, aiming for a month's cushion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty good, actually. A bit wary of the apps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you leave Meadowbank entirely?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If private work paid steadily for six months. Not before. I'm not reckless, I just like options.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at Meadowbank would struggle?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Lorraine, who's been there twenty years. She's brilliant with clients and hates her phone. I'd sit with her and show her, but she'd have to want to.

say: I'd say carers who **learn the tools** will be fine.
I'd offer to show Meadowbank colleagues **AI route planning**.
think: I think it **helps me** more than it hurts.
**Care-matching apps** make private work easier, but may take a big cut.
do: Join a **care-matching app** for weekend work, after checking fees.
Run a short **route-planning session** for colleagues.
Save private earnings towards **a month's cushion**.
feel: **Pretty good**, with some wariness about the **apps' fees**.
S1.quote: I'm not reckless, I just like options.
fieldNote: She sees **Steady Disruption** as an opening for private work.
Her caution is about **platform fees**, not technology itself.
She'd only leave the agency after **six steady months** of private work.

steps.text: Join a care-matching app for weekend private clients
Teach Meadowbank carers her AI route planning
Bank private earnings towards a month's cushion

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's fast. 2028 for the thinking, 2031 for the robots. Okay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people need to stop arguing about whether it's real and start getting ready. I'd say the government should help, but I wouldn't count on it in two years. I'd post practical stuff, like which courses are worth doing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think my day calls are gone by 2031, maybe sooner for the simple ones. But end-of-life care, sitting with someone who's dying, I think families will want a person for that for a long time. That's where I'd aim, and it's hands-on and human, not thinking work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd do the palliative care certificate through the hospice in town. I'd ask the hospice about bank shifts, so I'm known there. And I'd keep the private family work going to build some savings before 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, but I'd rather be scared and moving than scared and sitting still.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is the hospice really safer from robots?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know for sure. Nobody does. I sat with a dying client last spring for her last three nights. My client Mrs Hollis died holding my hand, and her son said that was what he remembered. I can't see a family choosing a robot for that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if the hospice had no shifts?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd move. Priya's been talking about going to the city anyway. There'd be more hospices and more work, and rent would be worse, but I'd take that.

say: I'd tell people to **stop arguing** and start getting ready.
I'd post **practical advice** about which courses are worth doing.
think: I think my **day calls are gone** by 2031.
Families will want **a person** at end of life for a long time.
do: Take the **palliative care certificate** at the hospice.
Ask the hospice for **bank shifts** to get known.
Keep **private family work** going to build savings.
feel: **Scared but moving**, rather than scared and sitting still.
S2.quote: My client Mrs Hollis died holding my hand, and her son said that was what he remembered. I can't see a family choosing a robot for that.
fieldNote: She bets on **end-of-life care** as the last place families accept robots.
She'd **move to the city** with her flatmate if local work dried up.
Her fear is real but **channelled into action**, fitting her adaptive style.

steps.text: Complete the palliative care certificate at the town hospice
Sign up for hospice bank shifts
Keep one private family for extra savings
Move to the city with Priya if hospice work dries up

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Okay, that's enough to do it properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a gift if you use it. I'd tell people at Meadowbank to pick one course and finish it, not to panic-scroll the news.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think five years lets me get into hospice work before the thinking AI even arrives. My day-call job goes around 2034, but by then I'd want to be on the hospice staff, not the bank. The money's still thin, though, so I can't afford a long unpaid gap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the palliative certificate next year and then apply for a permanent hospice care assistant post. I'd use AI to practise interview answers and to study. And I'd keep the private family for one weekend a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steady. Not calm, but like I know which way I'm walking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why not stay at Meadowbank until 2034?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the best hospice jobs go to people they already know. If I wait until everyone's panicking, I'm one of fifty hospice applicants. If I go now, I'm one of five.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does Priya think of all this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She thinks I'm mad for planning ten years ahead. Hairdressing feels safe to her. I'd tell her it's hands-on too, and that's not a free pass.

say: I'd say five years is **a gift** if you use it.
I'd tell colleagues to **finish one course** rather than panic-scroll the news.
think: I think I can get into **hospice work** before AGI arrives.
My **thin savings** mean I can't afford a long unpaid gap.
do: Do the **palliative certificate**, then apply for a permanent hospice post.
Use AI to **practise interviews** and study.
Keep one **private family weekend** a month.
feel: **Steady**, like she knows which way she's walking.
S3.quote: If I wait until everyone's panicking, I'm one of fifty hospice applicants. If I go now, I'm one of five.
fieldNote: She sees **moving early** as the main advantage of a five-year warning.
Her plan targets **permanent hospice staff** jobs.
She warns her hairdresser flatmate that **hands-on isn't safe** either.

steps.text: Apply for a permanent hospice care assistant post
Practise hospice interview answers with AI
Keep one private family weekend a month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is loads. I'd be thirty-seven when AGI arrives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is plenty of time, and anyone who wants to adapt can. I'd say employers should pay for training, because they'll save money on robots later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly I think I'd be fine, if I'm careful. Ten years is time to get into hospice work, maybe train as a nursing associate in palliative care. The only thing that could stop me is money, like the car dying when I'm halfway through a course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start with the palliative certificate and a few hospice bank shifts. I'd save a bit from the private family each month. And I'd keep using AI to learn faster than the course would teach me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good. Busy, but good.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if the car died?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ask Meadowbank for town-only rounds for a bit and take the bus. Or borrow from my dad, which I hate doing. I'd manage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd hold back on, with ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Moving to the city. With ten years, I'd rather stay near my dad, because he's on his own. I'd only go if I had to.

say: I'd say this is **plenty of time** for anyone who wants to adapt.
I'd say **employers should pay** for training, because robots will save them money.
think: I think I'd be **fine if careful**, moving into hospice work.
Only **money**, like the car dying mid-course, could stop me.
do: Start the **palliative certificate** and a few hospice bank shifts.
Save from **private family work** each month.
Use AI to **learn faster** than the course alone.
S4.quote: With ten years, I'd rather stay near my dad, because he's on his own.
fieldNote: A decade makes her **confident** about a hospice career.
With time, she'd **stay near her father** rather than move.
Thin savings remain her **one weak point**.

steps.text: Start the palliative certificate and hospice bank shifts
Put private family earnings into savings monthly
Study ahead of the course using AI

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because there's barely time to get trained before my day calls go. What would help is paid training places in hospices and palliative care, and a bit of help with fuel or a car so people in villages can actually get to the courses.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about the families who do the caring for free. When I do a respite week, the husband or daughter is usually exhausted. If robots ever help them, that would be the good side of all this.

headlineQuote: I'd rather be scared and moving than scared and sitting still.
portrait: Vera is a **27-year-old carer** doing village day calls and monthly live-in respite weeks.
She shares a flat, has a couple of weeks' **savings**, and drives up to forty miles a day.
She uses **AI every day**, for routes, mileage claims and learning sign language.
With faster AGI, she bets on **end-of-life care** as work families will keep human.
She is **pragmatic and centrist**, wanting employers to fund training rather than big promises.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, leaving barely time to train before day calls go.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid training places** in hospices and palliative care.
Help with **fuel or a car** so village carers can reach courses.
